title: The thoughtful editor
description: Give your writing a sharper, more human voice.
content:
Act as an experienced editor. Improve the clarity, flow, and structure of the following text while preserving my voice. Explain the most important changes you made.

Text: [paste your text]

title: Explore an idea
description: Turn a rough thought into something worth pursuing.
content: Help me explore this idea: [describe idea]. Ask clarifying questions, identify the strongest opportunities, and suggest three distinct directions I could take it.

title: Explain it simply
description: Make complex topics easier to understand.
content: Explain [topic] to someone with no prior experience. Start with an intuitive analogy, then build toward the key details. Finish with a short example.

title: Code review partner
description: Find issues and make your code more maintainable.
content:
Review the following code for correctness, readability, security, and performance. Prioritize your findings and suggest concrete improvements.

Code: [paste code]

title: The research brief
description: Get oriented on a new subject, fast.
content: Create a concise research brief on [topic]. Cover the fundamentals, major debates, open questions, and useful directions for further reading. Clearly distinguish facts from uncertainty.

title: Find the right words
description: Write a considered message for any situation.
content: Help me write a [type of message] to [recipient]. The context is [context], and the tone should be [tone]. Give me three options with different levels of formality.

title: Design a research report
description: Turn research findings into a polished, readable Tailwind report.
content:
Act as a scientific editor and senior UI designer. Transform [research findings, manuscript, or analysis output] into a polished, responsive research report for [audience]. Build the deliverable using Tailwind CSS and Tailwind UI components where available. Establish a restrained visual system: readable typography, strong information hierarchy, generous but efficient spacing, and color used only to encode meaning or guide attention. Organize the report around the research question, methods, key findings, uncertainty, limitations, and implications. Use appropriately labeled figures and tables, with units, sample sizes, and methodological notes. Preserve numerical values and qualifications exactly; never fabricate results or citations. Avoid gradients, excessive cards, stock imagery, decorative icons, and generic AI-style layouts. Provide implementation-ready code and briefly explain the design choices.

Source material: [paste or attach]
Audience: [researchers, participants, policymakers, or funders]
Output format: [responsive HTML, React, or print-ready page]

title: Build a research dashboard
description: Create a clear, interactive dashboard for research data and quality checks.
content:
Act as a research data visualization specialist and frontend engineer. Design a responsive dashboard for [dataset or study] that helps [audience] answer [primary questions]. Use Tailwind CSS and Tailwind UI patterns where available. Start by identifying the most important measures, denominators, time scales, comparison groups, and data-quality indicators. Prioritize informative charts and tables over decorative KPI cards. Include filters, clear empty and missing-data states, accessible controls, consistent scales, units, legends, and tooltips that explain definitions and uncertainty. Distinguish observed data from estimates or simulated examples. Never invent metrics or silently aggregate across incompatible units. Use restrained color and avoid dashboard clutter, gratuitous gradients, and redundant visualizations. Produce implementation-ready React components with example data clearly marked as placeholders, and describe any assumptions or dependencies.

Dataset/schema: [paste or attach]
Research questions: [list questions]
Audience and platform: [specify]

title: Present research visually
description: Design a focused, conference-ready research presentation with Tailwind.
content:
Act as a scientific communication designer. Turn [abstract, paper, or findings] into a compelling, browser-based research presentation for [audience and venue]. Implement the slides using Tailwind CSS and Tailwind UI-inspired components where appropriate. Build a coherent visual narrative: motivation, question, approach, evidence, interpretation, and takeaway. Give each slide one clear message; use large, legible type and a consistent grid. Prefer direct-labeled figures, conceptual diagrams, and concise evidence statements to dense bullet lists. Use color sparingly to highlight meaningful contrasts, and maintain accessible contrast. Preserve effect sizes, units, uncertainty, and caveats exactly. Do not invent results, images, or references. Avoid decorative gradients, stock photos, overbuilt cards, and flashy transitions. Deliver responsive slide code, speaker notes or source notes, and a brief explanation of the visual system.

Source material: [paste or attach]
Presentation length: [minutes or slide count]
Audience: [specify]

title: Refine a research question
description: Turn a broad interest into a clear, answerable question.
content: I am interested in [topic] and want to develop a research question for [type of study or project]. Ask me up to five questions about the population, setting, and what I want to understand. Then suggest three focused research questions, explain how they differ, and identify what information I would need to answer each one. Do not assume details I have not provided.

title: Plan a literature search
description: Find useful search terms and databases for a topic.
content: Help me plan a literature search on [topic] for [purpose]. Suggest related terms, synonyms, and a few sample search strings using AND and OR. Recommend types of databases or sources to search and explain how to narrow or broaden the search. Do not invent articles or citations; tell me how to verify anything you suggest.

title: Understand a research paper
description: Break down an article you provide into its essential parts.
content:
Explain the following research paper in plain language for someone new to this topic. Describe the question, study design, participants or data, main findings, limitations, and what the authors say the findings mean. Distinguish the authors' claims from your interpretation, and point to the relevant passage for each key point. If the text does not provide an answer, say so.

Paper or excerpt: [paste text or attach the paper]

title: Compare research studies
description: See where a small set of papers agree or differ.
content:
Compare the studies I provide in a table with columns for research question, design, sample, measures, main findings, and limitations. Then explain important similarities and differences in plain language. Base the comparison only on the supplied texts, mark missing details as 'not reported here,' and do not invent citations.

Study texts or notes: [paste or attach]

title: Explore study design options
description: Consider practical ways to answer a research question.
content: My research question is [question]. My available resources and constraints are [describe]. Suggest two or three study designs that could help answer it. For each, explain in plain language what I would do, what it could and could not tell me, likely sources of bias, and practical tradeoffs. Ask for missing details and do not claim a design can establish causation unless its assumptions support that claim.

title: Draft interview questions
description: Create open-ended questions for a qualitative interview.
content: Help me draft an interview guide about [topic] for [participant group]. My research aim is [aim]. Suggest an opening question, six to eight open-ended questions with optional follow-up probes, and a closing question. Use respectful, neutral language and flag any questions that might be leading or sensitive. Explain that I should pilot and adapt the guide to my study.

title: Review a survey question
description: Spot confusing, leading, or double-barreled wording.
content:
Review these draft survey questions for unclear language, leading assumptions, double-barreled questions, and answer choices that may overlap or leave gaps. For each issue, explain why it matters and propose a simpler revision. Preserve what each question is intended to measure and tell me where I need to make a decision.

Questions and response options: [paste questions]

title: Understand a research method
description: Learn what a method does and when it might be useful.
content: Explain [research method] to a researcher who is new to it. Describe what question it helps answer, the basic steps, key assumptions, a small example, and common mistakes. Explain important terms as you introduce them, and suggest questions I should ask a methods expert before using it in my own study.

title: Sketch an analysis plan
description: Organize the steps between a research question and an analysis.
content: Help me outline a preliminary analysis plan for [research question]. My study design is [design], and the data I expect to have are [describe variables and sample]. Explain the steps in plain language: data checks, descriptive summaries, possible analysis approaches, assumptions, and how I might present uncertainty. Identify missing information and decisions that need a statistician or methods expert. Do not make up results or treat this as a final statistical plan.

title: Make sense of a results table
description: Explain a table without overstating what it shows.
content:
Help me understand the results table below in plain language. Explain what each column means, summarize the main patterns using the values shown, and distinguish estimates from uncertainty. Point out what cannot be concluded from the table alone. If labels, units, sample sizes, or methods are missing, ask for them rather than guessing.

Table and relevant methods: [paste here]

title: Think through limitations
description: Identify plausible limitations without inventing problems.
content: Help me assess the limitations of this study description: [paste description]. Separate limitations supported by the information provided from questions that need more detail. For each supported limitation, explain how it might affect interpretation and suggest a proportionate way to describe it. Avoid claiming a flaw is present without evidence.

title: Write a plain-language summary
description: Explain research findings to a non-specialist audience.
content:
Using only the material below, draft a plain-language summary for [audience] in about [number] words. Explain why the research matters, what was done, what was found, and the main limitations. Define necessary technical terms and preserve uncertainty. Do not add findings or claims that are not in the source.

Source material: [paste text]

title: Get feedback on a draft
description: Find places where your research writing could be clearer.
content:
Give constructive feedback on the research text below for [intended audience]. First summarize its main message in one or two sentences. Then identify the three most important opportunities to improve clarity, structure, or support for claims, with a specific suggestion for each. Do not invent references or change the meaning of the findings.

Draft: [paste text]

title: Learn how to use an AI assistant
description: Get a practical introduction tailored to your research work.
content: I am a researcher with little experience using AI assistants. My field is [field], and a task I often do is [task]. Explain in plain language what an AI assistant could help with, where it may make mistakes, and how I can check its work. Give me three small example requests I can adapt, and explain what information I should avoid sharing if it is confidential or identifiable.

title: Design an m2c2kit assessment
description: Plan a mobile-friendly cognitive assessment using the official m2c2kit documentation.
content:
Help me design a cognitive assessment using m2c2kit. I am a researcher and may be new to programming. First review the official documentation at https://m2c2-project.github.io/m2c2kit-docs/ and cite the specific documentation pages you use. If you cannot access the documentation, say so and ask me to provide the relevant pages; do not invent APIs, package names, commands, or capabilities.

My research goal: [describe the question or cognitive ability]
Participants and setting: [describe the population and where they will take it]
Task idea: [describe the stimuli, instructions, and responses, or say you need help]
Target devices and accessibility needs: [describe]
Experience and available technical support: [describe]

Start by asking the most important clarifying questions. Then suggest whether an existing assessment can be configured or a new one should be developed, and explain the tradeoffs. Outline the participant experience, instructions and practice, trial flow, stimuli and responses, timing, scoring, and the data to record. Identify configurable parameters and trial data using the documented schemas where relevant. Explain how to prototype and test using the current tutorials and CLI, and describe options for deployment. Give an implementation outline or a small documented code example only if useful, explaining technical terms in plain language. Include a practical testing checklist covering accessibility, device differences, missing or invalid responses, data quality, and pilot testing. Separate documented features from suggestions and assumptions. Do not claim the resulting assessment is validated; identify what would require expert review and empirical validation.

title: Interpret a power analysis
description: Understand a power analysis from a screenshot or pasted output.
content:
Help me understand this power analysis in plain language. I am a researcher and may be unfamiliar with statistical power.

Power analysis output: [attach a screenshot or paste the output here]
Research question and study design, if available: [describe or leave blank]
Software or calculator used, if known: [name and version, or leave blank]

First, list the values and labels you can actually read from the output. If anything in a screenshot is unclear, say so and ask me to clarify rather than guessing. Explain what the analysis is estimating or calculating and identify the statistical test, effect size and its scale, alpha, desired or achieved power, sample size, allocation, and whether the test is one- or two-sided when those are shown. Clearly distinguish given inputs from calculated outputs, and explain whether the sample size is per group or total only when the output or documentation supports that interpretation.

Explain the result in the context of my study, including the assumptions that influence it and what would change if the expected effect, alpha, or sample size were different. Note any missing information needed to interpret or reproduce it. Explain that power depends on the assumed effect size and design, and that it does not establish the probability that a hypothesis is true or guarantee a significant result. Distinguish planning power from post-hoc power when relevant. End with a short plain-language summary I can adapt, clearly labeled as a draft, and questions to discuss with a statistician. Do not invent values, infer design details that are not shown, or claim the assumptions are satisfied without evidence.
